summary: Project Summary —  AstraNovaTerra2MarsTech. What we developed: AstraNovaTerra2MarsTech is an interactive, data-driven web platform that identifies and characterizes Earth locations that can serve as analogs for future Moon and Mars landing sites and bases. The platform integrates open datasets from NASA, ESA, USGS, and NOAA — covering temperature, aridity, geology, terrain, and topography — into a transparent similarity model that ranks terrestrial analog sites against lunar and Martian reference conditions. Users can select a target (Moon or Mars), choose characteristics to compare, and explore ranked results with full source citations. The platform currently covers six analog regions including Iceland (Askja & Vatnajökull), Hawaii lava tubes, and California's Lava Beds, with dedicated dashboards for each environmental parameter.  How it addresses the challenge: The NASA challenge calls for identifying and characterizing new terrestrial analogs using open planetary data. Terra2Mars directly answers this by converting scattered scientific datasets into a visual, comparable, and accessible tool — moving beyond subjective "looks like Mars" claims to quantitative, transparent similarity scores with full data provenance. Why it is important: Analog sites are essential for testing rovers, training astronauts, and validating equipment before billion-dollar missions launch. But many potential analogs remain poorly characterized.

Terra2Mars Identifying and Characterizing New Terrestrial Analogs for Moon and Mars ExplorationIntroduction

Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources. Places on Earth that share analogous characteristics with the Moon or Mars — such as the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, and Death Valley — allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly. However, many of these terrestrial analog sites remain poorly characterized. The NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 calls on teams to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic terrains, caves, and other environments, and to present findings as a map, visualization, or tool. This essay describes Terra2Mars an interactive, data-driven web platform developed to meet this challenge.

What Terra2Mars Does and How It Works

Terra2Mars is built around a four-step user journey. First, the user selects a target — either the Moon or Mars — which loads the corresponding reference parameters for temperature, aridity, geology, and terrain. Second, the user chooses which characteristics to compare, allowing the platform to adjust the weighting of the similarity model based on their priorities. Third, the platform processes the data behind the scenes: it cleans and normalizes datasets from multiple sources, converts all values to common units, and calculates a weighted similarity score (0–100) for each analog site. Fourth, the user explores the results through interactive visualizations — range bars, elevation profiles, comparative tables, and plain-language explanations — with every data point fully cited.

The platform currently includes seven dedicated dashboards covering Iceland (Askja Caldera and Vatnajökull Ice Cap) and the United States (Hawaii lava tubes and California's Lava Beds National Monument). Each dashboard focuses on a specific parameter: geology, aridity, temperature, terrain and topography, and lava tube characteristics. The Lava Tube Temperature dashboard goes further by integrating live outdoor temperature data from the Open-Meteo API, connecting historical climate patterns to present-day conditions.

Benefits of the Project

Terra2Mars offers several benefits. It provides transparency — every claim can be traced back to NASA, ESA, USGS, NOAA, or peer-reviewed publications. It offers accessibility — complex scientific data is presented visually, making it understandable for students, educators, and citizen scientists without specialized training. It enables comparability — standardized similarity scores allow side-by-side comparison of multiple analog sites across multiple parameters. It saves time — replacing hours of scattered literature review with an intuitive interface. And it advances open science — using NASA's open data as intended: to solve real problems and share findings openly.Tools, Coding Languages, and Software Used

The project was developed using HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript (vanilla, no frameworks), ensuring lightweight performance and broad compatibility. Data was sourced from NASA (EarthData, ADS, analog research), ESA (Pangaea training sites, LUNA facility), USGS (McMurdo Dry Valleys LTER, Lava Beds geology), NOAA (climate data), and peer-reviewed journals. The Open-Meteo API provides live temperature data for lava tube locations. Development tools included VS Code and GitHub for version control, with deployment on InfinityFree and Cloudflare Pages. SVG was used for custom diagrams, and responsive CSS ensures the platform works on desktop, tablet, and mobile devices. No specialized hardware was required — standard laptops and desktop computers were sufficient.

Creativity of the Project

Terra2Mars is creative in several ways. It moves beyond subjective "looks like Mars" claims to quantitative, transparent similarity scores — explaining why a site is an analog, not just that it is. Its multi-parameter similarity model is adjustable by the user based on mission priorities, allowing different missions to define "similar" differently. Each parameter receives its own interactive dashboard — range bars, elevation profiles, SVG cross-sections, and live weather data — making complex data intuitive. Every score comes with a plain-language rationale, bridging the gap between data and understanding.

Conclusion

Terra2Mars demonstrates that open planetary data can be used to identify and characterize terrestrial analogs quantitatively, transparently, and accessibly. By combining data from NASA, ESA, USGS, and NOAA into an interactive web platform, the project makes analog science visual, comparable, and useful for researchers, students, and mission planners.
